Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Pola Maneli’s Apart, written by Spike Lee, Tim Jones, Jeff Leisawitz, and Lubabalo Mtati. Made in association with Taking Over NY and 40 Acres and a Mule Filmworks, the film features music supervision by Black Coffee and wardrobe design by Laduma Ngxokolo. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning Best in Show at SIGGRAPH 2026.

Set in apartheid South Africa, Apart follows a forbidden friendship between two boys, tested by a life-saving act that forces them to confront the hatred dividing their world. Maneli draws on the visual language of anti-apartheid woodcut prints, combining rough lines and angular forms with harsh sunlight and shadows that evoke Nguni geometric patterns. Seen through a child’s eyes, the story connects an intimate relationship with the political system shaping it.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Pola Maneli: I loved that the script had the potential to hold space for deep emotional exploration of these characters as well as an acknowledgment of the political and sociocultural environment they existed in. I believe that the internal and external are inextricably linked, and exploring the reality of one can only deepen the understanding of the other.

I knew that I wanted to bring this supposed juxtaposition into sharp relief by telling the story through the eyes of our child protagonist.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

I did a lot of deep historical research prior to production, and despite being born and raised in South Africa, I was heartbroken by how comprehensive apartheid was in its brutality. The extent of the cruelty of those policies still isn’t adequately understood by the public. I also came across a handful of anecdotal testimonials from Black children during the period, and those affected me quite a bit as well.

As far as the process of filmmaking goes, being a first-time director meant that almost everything was a new lesson for me, and that meant having to absorb and process a lot of things on the fly. However, I was incredibly fortunate to have great support in the form of our animation production company, Colossal.

For example, as someone with a background in illustration, I pride myself on my drawing ability and stamina, so I think I initially tried to overcompensate for my lack of experience as a director by taking on a lot more technical tasks than I needed to. Thankfully, it didn’t take long for me to realize that this wasn’t the most efficient use of my time. Learning to loosen my grip and trust in my ability to express ideas to my collaborators through communication rather than execution was a big turning point early on.

There were quite a few learning moments like that.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I started out by looking at examples of live-action movies that were shot in high-humidity conditions that mimicked the feeling of a hot South African summer. From that, I knew that I wanted to have hard lighting with sharp shadows that would convey the feeling of an afternoon sun beating down directly on you.

From there, I felt there could be an opportunity to abstract those sharp shadows into geometric shapes that could be evocative of Nguni geometric patterns. I really liked the idea of using the light to allude to something geographic as well.

I knew that taking that approach to the lighting meant that the figures themselves would have to be fairly simple. We had a little bit of angularity in the figures, but not so much as to bring too much attention to itself and end up overwhelming the audience with “a hat on top of a hat,” so to speak.

The film draws on the visual language of woodcut prints used in anti-apartheid resistance. How did that historical connection influence your approach to the animation?

Visually, it meant that there was a certain degree of smoothness to the animation that I wanted to avoid. We achieved that by using hard, angular brushes in the background paintings wherever possible, as well as mostly animating on twos. We also tried to preserve a bit of roughness in the character linework to simulate the limitations of the medium when it came to depicting curved forms.

But at a storytelling level, those protest posters, for me, clearly showed that it was more than possible to reflect real-life circumstances without ever having to compromise on beauty—and that, in fact, beauty is an essential tool in giving your message the best possible chance of being spread as widely as possible.

Laika’s Wildwood grossed an estimated $9 million in its second weekend at the domestic box office, down just 27% from its debut frame and bringing its 10-day total to $27.4 million, according to updated figures distributor Fathom Entertainment sent out today.

Travis Knight’s stop-motion feature pulled in around $2.4 million on Friday and $2.7 million on Halloween Saturday, with Sunday sales climbing 38% to make it the film’s biggest day of the weekend and finish ahead of Fathom’s initial estimates.

Its second Sunday actually exceeded its opening Sunday by 2%, making it the day’s second-highest total ahead of Clayface.

Wildwood’s hold compares favorably when placed against previous Laika releases. Kubo and the Two Strings fell 37.8% in its second frame, ParaNorman declined 38.7%, and The Boxtrolls slipped 30.7%. As we wrote on Saturday, Wildwood also benefited from an expansion, with Fathom adding 150 second-weekend screens for a total of 3,103.

Audience polling offers further encouragement. According to PostTrak results supplied by Fathom, 96% rated the film excellent or very good, while 87% would definitely recommend it. That’s something to be excited about, especially with nearly one-third of those polled saying that positive word of mouth as a reason for buying a ticket over the weekend.

David Burke, Laika’s chief marketing and operations officer, said of the film’s sophomore performance:

Wildwood’s strong second-weekend hold is an encouraging sign of the staying power behind its exceptional audience response. Travis and the extraordinary team at Laika have created a film that audiences are embracing and enthusiastically recommending others experience in theatres. That response gives us real confidence as more moviegoers discover Wildwood in the weeks ahead.

Fathom CEO Jason Brenek added,

After partnering with Laika over the past decade to re-release films from its incredible catalog, Wildwood represents a landmark achievement for Fathom Entertainment. With an all-time high Fathom theatrical footprint and box office results tracking to meet or exceed the monumental success of our 2024 re-release of Laika’s Coraline for its 15th anniversary, Wildwood is demonstrating theatrical staying power; it’s a cinematic masterpiece, and we are heartened by its lasting box office appeal, exceptional audience reaction, and critical acclaim.

Against a reported $100 million production budget, Wildwood still has a long way to go, but as we’ve written previously, it’s a studio that, as much as any, doesn’t necessarily need immediate box office returns to justify its output. That said, the film’s second weekend and strong audience exit polling suggest that enthusiastic audiences can sustain its theatrical run beyond a modest opening, and that the studio may have another long-term fan favorite on its hands.

TOKYO, Japan— At TIFFCOM, the content market affiliated with the Tokyo International Film Festival, a session on Friday, October 30, examined Japanese animation’s global expansion from three perspectives.

Masahiro Hasegawa, editor-in-chief of the Anime Industry Report, opened with preliminary findings tracking the market in Japan and overseas. Hitomi Hiratsuka, director of international sales and productions at Nippon Animation, and Yoko Ueda, director of corporate administration and IP and communications at Production I.G, followed with observations on adapting to international partnerships and audiences.

Kazuko Ishikawa, president of both the Association of Japanese Animations and Nippon Animation, opened the session by saying that “recently Japanese animation is appreciated by many people worldwide […] the potential keeps on expanding.” She noted that many creators are developing works with overseas expansion in mind, emphasizing the “high expectations of the fans inside and outside of Japan.”

Session moderator Megumi Onouchi, president of HumanMedia and vice chair of the Association of Japanese Animations’ Human Resources Development Committee, later discussed the government’s New Cool Japan Strategy, which seeks to capitalize on this popularity.

Anime Isn’t Growing Equally

Preliminary figures for 2025, presented ahead of the Anime Industry Report 2026, showed international demand continuing to drive growth. The broader anime market—an estimate of consumer spending across anime and related products and services—reached ¥4.45 trillion ($28.22 billion), up 15.8% from 2024.

Overseas spending accounted for ¥2.54 trillion ($16.13 billion), up 17.2%, while the Japanese market grew 14.1% to ¥1.91 trillion ($12.09 billion). The overseas share consequently rose to 57.1%, compared with 56.5% in 2024.

The presentation distinguished this broader market from a narrower measure estimating anime production companies’ revenue. That figure reached ¥505.5 billion ($3.21 billion) in 2025, up 8.4%, with overseas revenue accounting for 27.9% of the total, compared with 25.5% a year earlier.

The distinction is important: the value of the wider anime business does not translate directly into revenue for the studios making the work. While animation is at the core of the business, merchandising, games, music, live entertainment, and other related activities also contribute to its overall value.

Japan’s content industry—which includes games, anime, manga, live-action film and television, and music—is targeting ¥20 trillion ($126.87 billion) in overseas sales by 2033, with anime expected to contribute ¥6 trillion ($38.06 billion).

Hasegawa cautioned that “international revenues do not necessarily come directly to the animation companies.” Money flows to production committees and is then distributed among their members, meaning the return to a studio can be smaller. Committee membership and investment arrangements vary from project to project.

Although production costs are rising, Hasegawa also noted that more production companies are retaining rights to their work, allowing them to benefit from domestic and overseas licensing revenue.

The presentation argued that Japanese anime’s presence among leading box office titles in various countries—with Demon Slayer offered as an example—and in global streaming rankings demonstrated an international breakthrough. The recognition of “anime” as a distinct category among international viewers is part of that development.

Hasegawa also discussed interest among survey respondents in expanding into emerging markets, including Africa. The handouts highlighted localization suited to local languages, cultures, and laws, alongside measures to combat piracy, as priorities for future growth.

How Nippon Animation and Production I.G approach overseas expansion

The second part of the session examined how Nippon Animation and Production I.G are putting international strategies into practice.

Hiratsuka opened with a presentation on Nippon Animation’s approach to reaching audiences around the world. She emphasized long-term development in new markets, alongside preserving older titles for exhibition.

She cited World Masterpiece Theater, explaining that its international outlook was unusual at the time and that its rigorous attention to detail helped give the series their lasting appeal.

“On the creative side, we cherished realism,” she said, highlighting location research for series such as Anne of Green Gables, which she described as “one of the most popular in Japan and across the world as well.”

“Regardless of the location of the audience, we wanted to create the common thread of the story where anyone anywhere can enjoy the story of each title [in World Masterpiece Theater].”

This led to a discussion of building titles’ long-term value through what Hiratsuka called a “life cycle”: viewers discover a series or film in childhood, retain their affection for it as adults, and pass that enthusiasm on to another generation.

“Through this longer-term strategy, we try to maximize the value” of each existing title, she said. Expanding that cycle into other countries is an important part of the studio’s international strategy.

Merchandising offers another way to sustain those connections, with examples including Seiko watch tie-ins, figurines, sweets, and Anne of Green Gables-themed desserts. Onouchi later underlined the point: “The past is not just about the past, but it’s still alive; there are fans still enjoying these works, so there is business still being generated.”

“We can never use a cookie-cutter approach; there is no one-size-fits-all approach,” Hiratsuka said, noting that different markets have distinct characteristics and interests.

International expansion should also be a two-way process, she argued, highlighting the importance of partners with different cultural and linguistic backgrounds in helping Nippon “expand the scope of our business activities.”

Hiratsuka reaffirmed the studio’s commitment to family-friendly animation despite declining birth rates. “There are still a great number of children in the world, and we will never stop having children,” she said.

Returning to the life-cycle concept, she argued that family-oriented animation is essential to developing “future supporters of the anime industry.”

Beyond the Screen

Ueda’s presentation approached international interest from a slightly different angle, though with some common ground. “Everything starts from the creation [of the anime],” she said. While maintaining that “it’s best to do as much as possible by ourselves,” she emphasized collaboration as central to Japanese anime’s future.

“Our strength is of course centered in the creation of videos and images,” Ueda said, explaining that co-production partners can contribute expertise and resources beyond the studio’s own capabilities.

“We are based in Japan, so there are things that we don’t know, and creators around the world have different resources,” she said. The aim is to combine Japanese anime aesthetics with that international knowledge.

“IP is not just about the work but the creators involved,” Ueda added, citing Production I.G’s animated sequence in Kill Bill as an example of successful collaboration. Its impact, she suggested, came from the combination of media: the same effect “would not be possible if Kill Bill was entirely animation.”

More recent work, including “The Ninth Jedi” for Star Wars: Visions, illustrates another type of partnership. Ueda described an interest in how Production I.G would interpret an established property, with the studio treated as a creative partner rather than simply a contractor.

“They are now looking at us as a partner [on] their creation,” she said. “We’re getting more offers of this kind”—working with “IP that came from outside of Japan […] amplified by the creativity of Japan.”

Ueda also stressed the importance of direct fan outreach: turning initial viewership into an ongoing relationship through live events and merchandising. She described these activities as common in Japan, with opportunities to develop similar connections overseas.

Events in the United States, Saudi Arabia, and India offered examples. In India, an activity that invited participants to trace drawings encouraged interest in the animation process while introducing fans to the people behind the work.

For Ueda, those encounters offer a way to deepen audiences’ connections with anime by building familiarity with its creators—extending the relationship beyond the screen.

After a brutal opening weekend that saw Bona Film Group’s Sanxingdui: Future Past, China’s first full AI-generated theatrical feature, make only around $180,000 from more than 10,000 screenings, the film has followed up with a similarly ignominious second weekend that gave no indication of a possible box office recovery.

According to the China Movie Box Office dashboard, at the time of writing, the film had earned roughly RMB1.68 million ($253,000) through Monday, November 2, its 11th day in theaters. Since our October 26 opening weekend report, the film has added only around $71,000 to its Chinese box office total.

Precise second-weekend totals aren’t available yet, at least not from our usual sources, but the film’s earnings over the intervening week mean it suffered a weekend decline of 60% or more.

The most optimistic Chinese market trackers now predict the film won’t even make back a third of its budget at the box office. Estimates cap out at around RMB3.07 million $460,000. That seems highly optimistic given the way the film fell off in week two.

According to reporting by Chinese outfit Jiemian, the “filmmakers” behind Sanxingdui produced the film to establish a viable pipeline for bringing genAI into feature filmmaking, and they believe they’ve done that. However, after recouping such a small fraction of the film’s budget, viability may not be the right word for what they proved.

Despite the losses, Bona is pressing ahead with more AI films. According to an October 29 Investment Times report published by Tonghuashun, the company has another AI science-fiction animated feature in production and a mythology-themed animated project in development.

The company may have proved that it can force AI-generated films into theaters and onto TV screens, but so far, it has done little to demonstrate that audiences are willing to pay for AI-generated content. While memes, TikToks, and Instagram reels may rack up huge viewing numbers, people are less willing to pony up real money to watch it in longer formats.

With a trio of the year’s buzziest animated feature credits under its belt – Jim Queen, In Waves, and Lucy Lost – Gao Shan Pictures has put together a cross-border operation based on the French island of Réunion that is quickly becoming the envy of the French indie animation scene.

Before this year’s impressive feature lineup, Gao Shan already boasted a heck of a resume, including work on films such as I Lost My Body, Mars Express, Sirocco and the Kingdom of the Winds, Little Nicolas, and many more, as well as shorts and series in both 2D and 3D, including The Smurfs and Team Nuggets. If there was a high-profile French indie on the festival circuit in the last decade, there’s a fair chance that Gao Shan was involved.

Twelve years after its founding by Arnaud Boulard, the company continues to expand while keeping local talent, environmental responsibility, and close creative partnerships at the heart of its approach.

Most recently, producers, investors, and artists flocked to the studio’s energetic pitch for Roots of My Hair at Cartoon Forum, in a standing-room-only pitch that was one of the event’s clear highlights. Gao Shan also took home the first Ecoprod-Cartoon Tribute, a new category in the established Cartoon Forum awards honoring sustainability efforts within European animation.

This sustainable, eco-conscious, and inclusive approach to making animation has been at the heart of Gao Shan’s policy, from the opening of its first studio on Réunion to its expansion with facilities in Angoulême, Mauritius, and, last year, Annecy.

Following the Ecoprod-Cartoon Tribute win, Cartoon Brew spoke with producers Anne-Flore Aussant and Bérangère Condomines, both at the core of Gao Shan’s current success.

“At Gao Shan, we choose projects based on Arnaud’s flair and ours,” explained Condomines. “Clearly, there’s an artistic vision we’re sensitive to. And then there are the values the films embody. For us, it’s important to pursue independent paths that, while having very interconnected topics, all reflect human values. So I think that naturally guides almost all our choices.”

The veteran producer, who grew up on Réunion, joined Gao Shan in 2021 to develop new in-house series and features. She quickly settled into the well-organized, supportive ecosystem Gao Shan had built with its many clients over the years. “It’s not only about the projects, it’s also about the people. We’re in fact very people-focused, and I think that shows not only in the stories we choose, but also in the people we partner with and the teams we build.”

Those teams include the staff in Annecy, supervised by Aussant alongside creative director Paul Ó Muiris. “Arnaud and I knew each other already, as I had worked with him on Réunion a little over eight years ago. He reached out back in 2022 as he wanted to develop a new facility in mainland France, and we got along incredibly well. Today, we are trying to start our first TV series in Annecy, and Bérangère is on the same path on Réunion, with Roots.”

With a collective shout of “Nappy hair matters!” Condomines and her creative team captivated Cartoon Forum’s audience with Roots of My Hair. The series, comprising six 13-minute episodes, embodies not only Gao Shan’s narrative DNA, but also the way it builds every project—with both a deep connection to the people involved and a skillful production setup.

“Roots is very similar to the projects we usually participate in as a service studio,” added Condomines. “It’s clearly defined, aligns with the worldview we want to put on screen, and we connected very much with the directors. Then comes the solution-finding process, and we’ve built a very good reputation around that particular aspect.”

For the two producers, having Gao Shan’s infrastructure and flexible teams at hand is a definite plus. The company boasts both 3D and 2D pipelines and can rely on experts in both techniques across all locations, as there’s no strict separation between facilities.

Building on this agility, Gao Shan weathered the storm of diminishing commissions and adapted to production demands. “We’re incredibly lucky to have teams in IT, pipeline, and all departments filled with artistic energy and ready to adapt to projects, stories, and the needs of our partners,” explained Aussant. “I think that definitely helped.”

“It’s not all rainbows and sunshine,” Condomines went on, “but I have the impression that what keeps us in shape is that we haven’t necessarily exceeded a critical size. We’ve seen in recent years that studios that suffered the biggest blows were way bigger than us. We managed to remain quite small, and I think perhaps we’re perceived as a much bigger company than we actually are. This size actually helped us, even if we’re not immune to these difficult times.”

Talent management is key to this adaptability and is also part of Gao Shan’s sustainable approach. On Réunion, 30% of the staff is now local, and the company partnered with the animation school Rubika to open a new campus there a few years ago. “The first students from this cohort are graduating next year, and we also work with another local school to take on interns every year. Our goal is to train as many talented people in the area as possible, not only to strengthen our capacity in the region but also to reduce our environmental impact,” explained Condomines.

At Gao Shan, environmental awareness and sustainability are more than just keywords, Condomines said. “Our approach can be split into three aspects. First, there’s the editorial line: we have a number of films that address ecological, environmental, or social issues.”

In 2024, the studio produced Pie Dan Lo, a short animated documentary by Kim Yip Tong about the 2020 oil spill off the coast of Mauritius, one of the region’s worst ecological disasters.

“Then, this awareness extends to the studio’s way of life,” continued the producer. “We have implemented a charter to facilitate eco-conscious best practices for everyone. And last but not least, that’s also something we think about when setting up a new production. Not only in terms of technique, pipelines, and software, but also in terms of talent and where people are based, as I mentioned earlier.”

Thousands of miles from mainland Europe, this regional hub—encompassing Réunion, Mauritius, and Madagascar—continues to grow, with Gao Shan part of an effort to support not only local artists, but storytellers as well.

“There’s a real common desire to showcase the talent of the region,” concluded Aussant, who praised her colleague’s project Roots of My Hair more than once during the interview. “After all, it’s a completely unique geographical area, with great potential and great people. When you’re in this field, it’s crucial, and I would say that it’s what kept us going also when times were tough. If you’re surrounded by good people and you work with supportive ones, it does help you get through it.”

Kojima Productions has released a new teaser and story details for Death Stranding Isolations, its upcoming hand-drawn animated series set in Hideo Kojima’s post-apocalyptic video game universe. The studio also announced that popular sci-fi author Tow Ubukata is handling series composition and screenwriting.

The studio unveiled the update during its 10th anniversary celebration at Tokyo’s Azabudai Hills Gallery. The series is scheduled to premiere sometime in 2027 on Disney+.

Directed by Takayuki Sano, Isolations is being animated in traditional 2D by E&H Production, whose credits include Ninja Kamui and Bullet/Bullet. Kojima serves as executive producer, with original character designs by Ilya Kuvshinov.

The series delivers an original story set in the same world as Kojima’s games, where encounters between the living and the dead have triggered catastrophic explosions, which leave survivors scattered and isolated. Its new synopsis opens with a blunt introduction to that reality: “My mom became a crater.”

Set in North America, protagonist Sam reconnects the continent through the Chiral Network. Isolations explores the unforeseen consequences of those renewed connections. At its center is a woman who has grown to embrace solitude, rejecting opportunities for human contact until chance encounters pull her into an unfamiliar world.

In a release following the announcement, Sano described the responsibility he felt in extending Kojima’s established world:

One of the unique abilities of entertainment is its power to enhance the spirituality of those who consume it, and I think this is something that Mr. Kojima’s works have always achieved. As a result, I approached this production with an exceptionally strong sense of duty and responsibility. I knew that no matter what, I needed to accomplish the same thing.

Ubukata’s addition comes with significant sci-fi clout. His novel, Mardock Scramble, won the Nihon SF Taisho Award in 2003, while his historical novel Tenchi Meisatsu received Japan’s Booksellers’ Award in 2010. His work spans novels, games, comics, and animation.

First announced last November, Isolations is one of several animated expansions of the franchise. Kojima Productions has also announced the anime feature Death Stranding: Mosquito, directed by Hiroshi Miyamoto at ABC Animation Studio, and an adult animated feature developed with Los Angeles-based Line Mileage.

Spain’s Arriate Studio and Mexico’s ¡Viva Calavera! are bringing Halloween and Christmas together in Samhain, an animated feature in development based on Lobón Leal’s popular 2024 graphic novel.

Leal and María Luquero are co-directing, with Leal also handling art direction and adapting his book for the screen. Calavera Hermanos are co-producing and leading animation direction.

Just in time for Halloween, we’re excited to debut the project’s first trailer below:

The fantasy adventure is Arriate’s first feature project and brings together the young Andalusian company with the buzzy Mexican studio behind Cartoon Network Latin America’s hugely popular Rey Mysterio vs. The Darkness series. The planned film will run roughly 90 minutes, mixing 2D and 3D animation for a young adult audience.

Samhain follows Mika, a young magical creature who dreams of finding a land of candy beyond the border separating her forest home from the human world. When she, her brother Miko, and their friend Frigo discover a crashed sleigh, they cross that border into a barren, colorless world where magic and nature are exploited for profit.

There, they meet Miss Allsaints, a witch who makes money from magic, and Don Papi, the film’s unique version of Santa Claus. Drawing on folklore and fairy tales, the adventure explores how Halloween and Christmas have become big business, and what that means for the natural world.

Based in Chiclana de la Frontera, Cádiz, Arriate is involved in animation production, original project development, and illustrated-book publishing. Leal and Luquero founded the studio alongside executive producer Cristina Fernández. Their previous credits include Spain’s biggest TV (Pocoyo) and film (Tad the Lost Explorer) IPs.

According to the studio founders, its mission is to support artist-led projects and create more opportunities outside Spain’s established animation hubs of Madrid and Barcelona. With Samhain, that means taking a homegrown comic to the screen with an international partner. Of the Samhain project, they tell us:

This is exactly the kind of milestone we dreamed of when we created Arriate Studio. Building original stories from the periphery, bringing creative projects to life from our corner of the world, and watching them grow hand in hand with friends is what makes this journey so special and worthwhile.

Founded in 2014 by the habitually-masked Los Hermanos Calavera, ¡Viva Calavera! specializes in concept development, storyboarding, directing, and visual development for animation, games, and comics. Its Rey Mysterio series, co-produced with Cartoon Network Latin America and the legendary luchador himself, mixes lucha libre, supernatural adventure, Mexican culture, and anime influences. The studio developed its scripts, storyboards, and conceptual designs, working with production partners across Latin America.

Speaking with us about their new feature project, Los Hermanos Calavera told us:

Collaborating with Arriate on Samhain has been fantastic. Across an ocean, we share sensibilities and the hunger to make something interesting and unique. Lobón’s art and aesthetic sense work very well with our animation style, and we’re excited to bring this story to life beyond the comic book pages.

Leal’s original 308-page book mixes color and black-and-white imagery, laying the visual groundwork for the film. The settings are a big part of that world, with the magical forest standing in stark contrast to the barren landscape beyond the border.

Global Music Branding composed the teaser’s music and will stay involved as the project develops. A release date for the feature has not yet been announced.

TOKYO, Japan – Tokyo Anime Next presented a special animation symposium at TIFFCOM this week, Toward the Launch of a New Anime Award in 2027, exploring the importance of establishing a new international award recognizing Japanese animation. The award will have an online component and is intended to reach overseas audiences as much as domestic audiences.

Moderating the symposium was TIFF animation programming advisor Ryota Fujitsu. Joining him as panelists were Yuichiro Saito, a Studio Chizu producer on The Girl Who Leapt Through Time, Summer Wars, and Wolf Children; Akira Shimizu, director of the Association of Japanese Animations and president and representative director of A-1 Pictures Inc.; and Masaya Saito, chief manager of the animation division and planning group leader at Toho Co., Ltd.

Fujitsu emphasized that the panel did not constitute an official announcement of the award, which will come next year. Instead, he and the panelists took the opportunity to discuss their hopes for the changes the award might inspire in their industry.

Masaya Saito reflected on the significance of Japanese experts selecting works for such an award. “Peer review can facilitate networking and provide mutual inspiration within the industry. There are more than 300 TV series and 80 film titles in any given year — no one can watch all of them — but we can collectively evaluate these works by employing diverse individuals; it takes the entire industry.”

The principal purpose of the new international award is to communicate the advancements and achievements of the anime industry more directly to the world at large — “how it has become optimized such that people around the world can now enjoy it,” explained Masaya Saito. “Anime is the most globally localized entertainment across different cultures and languages. By assessing it, we want to communicate that reality more directly. And I want international audiences to discover what Japanese audiences are enjoying.”

Studio Chizu’s Yuichiro Saito views the Japaneseness of anime as a disruptor within the global cultural equation. “The world is composed of two major trends,” he said. “European art history, film and fine art generated from that value system and aesthetic lineage, and an aesthetic and value system centered in the U.S. which has a global reach. If we say that [anime] is from Japan, from Asia, we interject a third element into this previously two-element world. I hope this kind of aesthetic communication can be furthered by this award.”

Yuichiro Saito reflected on how his peers in the anime industry came together to crowdfund aid in the wake of the California wildfires two years ago. It speaks not only to his industry’s sense of community, but also to whom it now reaches. “Japanese anime’s uniqueness can demonstrate how connected the world is. Borderlessness is very important in the presentation of our works.”

Moved by the other panelists’ remarks, Akira Shimizu said that he views “going global” as a big responsibility and a core mission. He said the award could help define and communicate the context of Japanese anime’s creation — the unique skills and technology involved. Drawing on his experience as a studio director, Shimizu reflected on current trends in production pipelines. “Now that anime are streamed internationally, fantasy and action works are popular,” he said. “We’re often asked: ‘A-1 Pictures, can you please make a fantasy action work?’ One of the appeals [of anime] is the diversity of genre and aesthetic, and we should carry this forward into the future. I’m interested in making romance works! But action fantasy is popular around the world, and so we should make it. But is that enough? We should interrogate that.”

Fujitsu asked the panelists what expectations and hopes they had for the award’s impact in 10 years’ time.

Masaya Saito said that critical mass is needed. “When launching any anime project, we emphasize that it has to be new in itself, and it has to be emotive, or empathetic,” Saito reflected. “And I think we should have a third perspective as well in evaluating creators — industrial empathy, to nurture creators.”

Shimizu wants the next generation to have something to reach for. “In 10 years’ time, I will be well retired, but in the future there is one thing I would like to focus on — those entering the industry should aspire to this award; that is what I would like for the next generation.”

Laika’s Wildwood has passed $20 million in North America after eight days, with distributor Fathom Entertainment projecting a $7–8 million second weekend. That would push its total past $25 million through Sunday.

Travis Knight’s stop-motion feature earned approximately $2.4 million on Friday, with roughly 200 screens still to report. That’s down about 18% from its opening Friday, excluding previews.

The full weekend projection points to a 35–43% decline from its $12.3 million debut, a respectable hold roughly in line with earlier Laika releases.

Kubo and the Two Strings offers the clearest comparison: it opened to $12.6 million in 2016 before dropping 37.8% to $7.8 million in its second weekend. That said, Laika’s two preceding films started bigger and held as well or better: ParaNorman fell 38.7% after a $14.1 million debut, while The Boxtrolls slipped 30.7% after opening to $17.3 million.

Fathom also added 150 screens for Wildwood’s second weekend, bringing the film to 3,103 across the U.S. and Canada. That expansion will surely contribute to the film’s hold, wherever it lands.

Along with today’s numbers, Wildwood producer and Chief Marketing and Operations Officer at Laika, Dave Burke, said:

We made Wildwood for audiences who love bold, imaginative cinema, and our ambition has always been to expand the traditional family audience. We trust audiences to embrace a film that takes risks, both in the story it tells and how it’s made. Passing $20 million in eight days, alongside an ‘A’ CinemaScore, gives us confidence as we continue bringing Wildwood to more moviegoers. This is a film made to be experienced on the big screen, and we’re proud to see audiences relishing it.

As we reported after its debut, Wildwood earned an A CinemaScore. Its early audience reception and second-Friday performance are encouraging, although the projected weekend result would put it in familiar territory for Laika rather than mark an unusually strong hold.

There’s still plenty of ground to cover against a reported $100 million production budget. The film appears to be avoiding a steep second-weekend fall, but building a substantial theatrical run from its modest opening will take more than one decent hold. Laika’s films can have a long commercial life, as Coraline has demonstrated, but it’s too early to know whether Wildwood will follow that path.

International collaboration takes center stage in our second dispatch from the Tokyo International Film Festival, where international producers discuss how to bring animated projects across borders, and Ervin Han offers a closer look at an upcoming feature putting those ideas into practice.

In a TIFFCOM panel, Han joined Taiki Sakurai (Salamander Pictures) and Ilan Urroz (Foliascope) to examine the opportunities and challenges of international co-production, from financing structures to finding partners with complementary strengths. Their discussion highlighted the differences between Europe’s extensive public funding systems and Asia’s reliance on private investment, as well as the creative possibilities of connecting artists across countries.

Han also spoke with us about A Banquet for Hungry Ghosts, an animated horror anthology bringing together studios from Singapore, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Ireland. Following the Annecy success of The Violinist, the producer is developing four tales built around Chinese dishes, with distinct visual approaches and a shared ambition: make the food look delicious before things turn horrifying.

Expanding into the festival’s feature lineup, we spoke with the filmmakers behind four titles in Tokyo’s lineup about their craft. Atsushi Nishigori explores the contrasting styles of Grotesqqque, while Masanao Kawajiri breaks down Cherry and Virgin’s inventive combination of manga imagery and rotoscoping. TOKYO, Japan — Recent years have seen more co-productions in anime, and there is clearly a growing curiosity about the potential for features to find extra support outside Japan.

A session at TIFFCOM on Thursday, October 29, described international co-production as “anime’s new frontier.” The panel, moderated by Masao Kawano, program manager at Into Global, included Ervin Han, co-founder and CEO of Robot Playground Media and co-director of recent Annecy winner The Violinist; Foliascope CEO Ilan Urroz; and Salamander Inc. CEO Taiki Sakurai, a producer whose screenwriting credits include Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex.

The talk was split into three distinct parts, covering the “key challenges and opportunities of international co-production,” financing models and deal structures, and going to market. Han spoke first, mentioning that TIFFCOM was where he met a co-producer as well as the composer on The Violinist. He then discussed his aims for Robot Playground, looking to find “culturally-rooted stories from Asia and introduce it to a global audience.”

Han took a moment to introduce Robot Playground’s new project, The Banquet for Hungry Ghosts, showing a trailer for one of the anthology’s stories, Egg Fried Rice. Han noted that, somewhat similarly to The Violinist, Banquet will be a “majority Asian co-production with minority European components,” with production across Singapore, Malaysia, Taiwan, and Ireland. “So the production studios are based around Southeast Asia,” Han said, “and Ireland looks after music and audio posts as a minority partner.”

After Han’s quick briefing on his ongoing projects, Urroz introduced Foliascope’s work as well as the project the company would be pitching at the Tokyo Gap Financing Market, Back to Tomioka. Urroz highlighted co-production partners in Poland, Hungary, and Belgium, as well as creatives from Japan. “That’s exactly what we want to achieve with this movie: mixing the culture, mixing the artists coming from France, from Europe, from Japan, living in a different country but sharing the same spirit; animation can be the medium to turn to any audience about feelings, about love, about friendship.”

Urroz noted that the company was already developing marketing around the film, with merchandise including a board game designed by Antoine Bauza. Foliascope has also sold the film’s subscription streaming rights to Crunchyroll, with the companies working together to release a Japanese version.

The Foliascope CEO pivoted to discussing French systems for co-production, which the panel moderator had described as “enviable” at the opening of the session. “We are super lucky in France,” Urroz said. “We have public funding for lighting, development, production, also [innovation] funds for our studio or pipeline, we have also this incredible fund for foreign production cinematography. You can be from any country in the world: if you have a co-producer in France for a little part, you can ask for money from the French system.”

“Of course, with the internationalization of production, we have also the international tax credit. It’s a tax rebate, but we have also this very very useful paper visa, talent visa,” he continued. Urroz pointed out that in America, it is much more difficult to bring in a crew from another country to work for one to three years, and said the process in France is faster. “We made the stop-motion animation feature film The Inventor with Jim Capobianco, a veteran of Disney and Pixar,” Urroz said, adding that the production used the international tax credit.

Urroz also said these funds enable studios to embrace sustainable production. “With the French system, we are capable of transforming all our studios into positive generating solar studios, all our productions are made with solar energy,” he said. “It’s an incredible fund, an incredible system, but totally open for foreign co-production.”

Urroz also pointed to Creative Europe’s MEDIA program. “We have 27 countries in the European space, but it’s open to other countries around Europe,” he said. “It’s a system that directly helps the development of new feature films, up to 60,000 euros by co-producer, and you can have up to four co-producers […] then after you can ask for an image fund that also provides some funds for distribution, for marketing, etc.”

“The very basic difference between financing in Asia and Europe is the fact that in Europe, as even a solution, you know, in some ways they are very fortunate to have a very established, structured system for financing, particularly within the EU, to the extent that a majority of the budget could be financed if it’s you know, structured the right way through soft monies, incentives, and grants, and broadcaster pre-sales,” Han said.

“In Asia, most of it is private financing. This is a fundamental difference that I’ve actually found sometimes requires quite a bit of understanding for Asia to co-produce with Europe. In Asia, there is some amount of government financing, but by and large, I think it’s maybe up to 20% at most, if you’re lucky. And the majority has to be raised privately through structured financing, through private equity, sometimes specific private equity investors, family offices.”

Asked about the pros and cons of international co-production for anime, Sakurai said he felt Japanese animation was still viewed from a narrow perspective, which complicates funding when certain expectations are tied to the term “anime.” At the same time, he has found a “high level of tolerance” when a project aligns with those expectations.

Following the other panelists’ points about government support, Sakurai highlighted that even the greatest successes are generally not made overnight. He referred to the success of Makoto Shinkai—a director he called a “genius”—who also needed many chances to break through and succeeded following 14 years of support from his producer.

Han went on to say that one real challenge for many producers in Asia is securing support from broadcasters. “It’s also why we have to go overseas. I mean, the whole idea of a [co-production] is that it’s not just finding money; it’s finding partners with complementary strengths and partners who believe in your story, in your film, in your tv series, in your project. To do it together because you cannot do it alone. You know, I think that principle is very important. Once their understanding is there, then we try to find a way.”

Just as TIFFCOM as a whole suggested a general interest in co-production, the panel showed the financial incentives driving that interest, alongside Japanese companies’ hopes of deepening their connections with global audiences. Urroz and Han’s observations highlighted a key attraction: the more extensive government support available in countries such as France compared with financing systems in Asia.

Adorable pink bears are the main attraction at Pinkooland, a theme park whose biosynthetic mascots offer visitors an encounter with something fluffy, friendly, and engineered to entertain. For the people working below ground, however, keeping that fantasy running is a considerably less appealing proposition.

With Halloween just around the corner, Cartoon Brew is debuting the trailer for director Luis Usón’s 12-minute animated short, an Ecuadorian-Spanish production that brings horror, science fiction, and corporate satire into a world built around manufactured happiness. The film recently premiered in the official short film competition at the Sitges International Fantastic Film Festival of Catalonia, and functions as a potential entry point into something far more ambitious.

Watch the trailer below:

The story follows Kassy, a park employee trapped in its underground facilities when the Pinkoos, those seemingly lovable bears, unleash chaos and destruction. It’s a premise with an immediately apparent appeal in an era of indie horror box office dominance.

“Packed with action, suspense, and ultra-violence, it’s a mind-bending journey that explores the dark and disturbing corners of ourselves and the society we live in, where pink teddy bears, ruthless corporations, and childhood dreams collide in an explosive and, above all, insanely fun experience,” Usón explains.

Produced by Ecuador’s Matte CG and Spain’s Vanova, Pinkooland brings together artists with backgrounds in animation, VFX, and video games. Usón’s experience includes layout and previs work on major studio productions, including Denis Villeneuve’s Dune. He previously co-directed the animated short Afterwork with Pinkooland producer and CG supervisor Andrés Aguilar, Ichi to his friends.

“Pinkooland is the film I’ve always dreamed of making,” Usón says. “A film for those who want to dive into a different, unexpected, and dangerous world.”

The creative team also includes animation director Cécile Brossette, whose credits include The Lorax, Despicable Me 2, and Minions, and production designer Enric Sant, who came to animation after more than a decade in video games. Usón wrote the short with María Burgués and Omar Rabuñal Varela.

For the performances, Usón worked with an actress using motion capture to develop the characters’ movements and physical interactions. That material provided a foundation that the animators refined through keyframe animation. Detailed previs and 3D layout established staging, camera movements, and timing before the team moved into final animation.

Using Unreal Engine, the filmmakers adjusted lighting, cameras, materials, and environments interactively. The team also handled hair simulation within the engine, while using Houdini for complex visual effects.

More than a standalone short, Pinkooland was also conceived as a proof of concept for a feature currently in development. Alongside introducing Kassy and the park’s unsettling universe, it gave the filmmakers an opportunity to test the production pipeline for a longer film combining horror, science fiction, and dark comedy.

For now, the trailer introduces a workplace where the cheerful branding promises far more comfort than the employees can expect.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Vinnie Ann Bose’s Sulaimani, a French production from Girelle Production and Les Astronautes. Bose’s first professional film combines stop-motion for its present-day scenes with hand-painted 2D animation for memories. It earned Oscar qualification through wins for Best Short Film at the 2025 Manchester Animation Festival and the animation jury award at the 2026 Aspen Shortsfest.

At an Indian restaurant in Paris, two women from Kerala encounter familiar flavors, sounds, and smells that stir memories of the country they left behind. Their reasons for leaving differ, as do their relationships with home. Drawing on Bose’s own experience moving to France, Sulaimani explores food as both a source of comfort and a connection to complicated histories of family, identity, and independence.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Vinnie Ann Bose: I am from Kerala, just like the two protagonists of the film. I moved to France in 2016 to study, and I started writing Sulaimani in 2018. It was a time when I was feeling very homesick. During difficult days, food from home was a big source of comfort. Sulaimani began with a simple craving for a Kerala restaurant in France.

Meanwhile, I was slowly starting to feel comfortable in France, which made me question my identity and my relationship with both countries. Sulaimani was a way for me to think through these questions and find some clarity in my life choices.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

Sulaimani is my first professional film. The production was a wonderful experience, where I learned how to direct a team, collaborate with numerous talented artists to improve the film, and experiment with techniques that I had never tried before.

But the most valuable lesson was how to find the right distance when the film’s subject is so personal. This was the biggest challenge during the script and storyboard phase, creating an emotional roller coaster until I was satisfied with the animatic. Everything that followed seemed like a walk in the park in comparison.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I wanted to use two animation techniques to distinguish the present from the past. Stop-motion feels tangible and realistic, which I felt suited the present. I believe that memories are often shaped by our emotions rather than by facts. So I felt that 2D animation, with its hand-painted images and exaggerated colors, would help retain a certain imperfection and ambiguity, just like our memories.

I wanted the characters to have subtle and natural acting, so I decided on a realistic animation style. The character design was developed accordingly, to allow subtle expressions while remaining recognizable across both animation styles.

Food plays such an important role in the film. What were the biggest challenges in bringing its textures, preparation, and sensory qualities to the screen?

It was important to me to make the food look edible and delicious, even in miniature, as it is the heart of the film. But it was very tricky to make the food look appetizing!

We used the weirdest things, like hair gel with tiny pearls to create boiling water, plastic wrap to simulate tea being poured into a glass, papier-mâché to make the porottas, and glycerin to make the chicken curry shine. It took a lot of trial and error before we reached a satisfying result.

Patrick Stewart, whose unmistakable voice brought weight to animated kings, sexually charged absurdity to some of television’s most disreputable authority figures, and dignity to a talking poop, died Wednesday, October 28, at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.

His spokesperson said he had been living with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. His death was announced Thursday.

Known best as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, Stewart built an extensive animation career alongside his world-class performances onstage and in live action. His credits stretched from The Plague Dogs and The Prince of Egypt to The Simpsons, American Dad!, and English-language versions of films by Hayao Miyazaki and Katsuhiro Otomo.

Stewart was also an outspoken admirer of the medium. In a 2011 CNN interview, he offered an endorsement that went well beyond his own voice acting work:

I think in film the most exciting work currently is being done in animation.

Animation offered Stewart opportunities to extend the qualities audiences recognized from his famous screen characters, and, by his own account, gleefully dismantle them. He would regularly make audiences, and himself, break out into giggling fits when discussing some of his more absurd animation roles.

One of Stewart’s earliest voice acting feature credits was Major in Martin Rosen’s devastating The Plague Dogs (1982). Adapted from Richard Adams’s novel, the film belonged to a very different tradition from the family entertainment that would account for much of his later feature work.

In 1994, he voiced Adventure, the swaggering, pirate-styled book in the live-action/animated cult favorite fantasy The Pagemaster. Joining a voice cast that included Whoopi Goldberg, Frank Welker, and fellow Star Trek alum Leonard Nimoy, Stewart helped turn literary genres into physical characters.

A more imposing assignment followed when DreamWorks cast him as Pharaoh Seti in The Prince of Egypt (1998). Stewart gave the ruler the conviction of a man who considered his authority and the violence used to preserve it entirely natural. His ability to convey paternal affection alongside moral blindness lent dramatic weight to the fledgling studio’s ambitious first hand-drawn feature.

His feature career also encompassed broad comedy and science-fiction adventure. He voiced the alien King Goobot in Jimmy Neutron: Boy Genius (2001), teacher Mr. Woolensworth in Disney’s Chicken Little (2005), and Max Winters in the CG feature TMNT (2007).

For English-speaking audiences, Stewart also appeared in two modern classic anime features. He played the swordsman Lord Yupa in the 2005 English-language dub of Hayao Miyazaki’s Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind and inventor Lloyd Steam in the English version of Katsuhiro Otomo’s Steamboy.

His famous Shakespearean stage career took an animated turn in 2011’s Gnomeo & Juliet, where he voiced a statue of The Bard himself.

On TV, one of his defining guest performances arrived in the 1995 Simpsons episode “Homer the Great.” As Number One, leader of the Stonecutters, Stewart presided over a secret society whose elaborate rituals disguised a collection of petty privileges and childish grievances.

Stewart’s longest-running TV animation role came when he was asked to voice CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock in American Dad! Stewart began voicing Stan Smith’s boss when the series launched in 2005, lending the character his voice and likeness for the next two decades.

Bullock turned Picard and Xavier’s authority inside out. He was reckless, vindictive, sexually uninhibited, and spectacularly unfit to wield the power he possessed. Stewart’s assured delivery made the character’s behavior even more outrageous, as did the absurdity of a senior CIA official sounding unmistakably British. Stewart joked that the writers had promised him a scene in which the other agents would finally notice his accent, a development he suggested would signal the end of the series.

Stewart spoke warmly about the role and the people behind it, describing American Dad! as a source of extraordinary professional pleasure:

It has given me as much pleasure as almost anything in my career, not just because the writing is brilliant and scabrous and offensive and provocative, but because the people themselves are such adorable people.

MacFarlane, a longtime admirer and collaborator of Stewart’s, mourned the loss of his friend on Instagram, writing:

Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us.

I grew up as a fan, and was later gifted the privilege of becoming a colleague and friend, working with him for many years on “American Dad!”, “Family Guy”, and “Ted”. He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come. I remember exchanging emails with him a number of years ago when he was beginning day 1 of a new film. He commented to me that he always walked onto a new set feeling like the biggest novice there. My stunned reaction was the same as anyone’s would be. I said, “Patrick, if you feel that way, the rest of us are screwed.” We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet.

His most recognizable live-action characters also followed him into other forms of animation. Robot Chicken brought him back as Gurney Halleck, his character from David Lynch’s Dune, while games offered repeated returns to Picard and Professor Xavier. His Xavier performances included X-Men Legends and X-Men Legends II: Rise of Apocalypse; his Picard credits included Star Trek: Armada, Bridge Commander, and Legacy. Beyond those franchises, his game work included Emperor Uriel Septim VII in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and Zobek in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

His appetite for incongruity remained intact in The Emoji Movie (2017), where he voiced Poop. Appearing on Conan, Stewart explained that accepting the part reflected his “philosophy of finding diversity in the work that I do.”

“Thirty years ago, I probably wouldn’t have accepted this role. But I am now honored and delighted to be playing the role of the emoji poop.”

The character, he explained, would be “a very upright, very proper, rather cultivated sounding Englishman.” Stewart clearly enjoyed the absurdity of the assignment, recalling his enthusiastic response when his agent revealed the offer: “How diverse could an emoji role get? Poop is it. That’s the one.”

Born July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. Star Trek: The Next Generation, which premiered in 1987, made him an international star; the X-Men films brought another defining role beginning in 2000. Across those decades, animation became a recurring outlet for both his dramatic skill and his increasingly visible comic appetite.

He is survived by his wife, singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, and his children, Daniel and Sophia.
